title: Practical room-temperature superplastic forming of common alloys

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical way to shape affordable, common metal alloys into complex components at room temperature by allowing exceptionally large, controlled deformation without premature failure. Superplasticity would provide the material’s capacity to stretch; a manufacturing process would turn that capacity into repeatable forming of large parts at commercially useful rates. The intended scope includes aluminum or ferrous feedstock, although the supplied experimental evidence concerns a particular aluminum–zinc alloy.

As a proposed capability definition, success requires the combination of affordable alloy chemistry, suitable feedstock dimensions, stable and reproducible microstructure, useful forming speed and acceptable finished properties. Exceptional elongation in a miniature tensile specimen establishes a material behavior, but does not by itself establish this manufacturing capability. Room-temperature forming also describes the shaping stage: feedstock preparation and subsequent treatment may still require heat or demanding mechanical processing.

significance.text: If achieved across useful common alloys, the capability would offer a substantial new route to complex, near-net-shape metal components. Avoiding elevated temperatures during forming could reduce forming-stage heating, while sufficiently capable shaping could replace some fabrication operations. The supplied paper connects its laboratory result to the possibility of shaping nanostructured materials into their final form at room temperature; it does not demonstrate a production process or quantify manufacturing savings.

System-level synthesis: lighter structures, fewer joined assemblies, lower total energy use and lower total cost are conditional downstream possibilities. They depend on which operations the process can replace, the cost and energy of preparing the feedstock, tooling requirements, production yield, any subsequent treatment and the performance of the finished part. Easy deformation alone does not establish a better structural component or a cheaper production route.

A central limit is the relationship between formability and structural performance. The paper explicitly notes that room-temperature superplasticity reduces flow stress, which is undesirable for many structural applications, and discusses subsequent homogenization or aging as ways to increase it. Thus, room-temperature shaping should not be equated with an entirely room-temperature production chain. Transfer from the tested Al–Zn system to ordinary commercial aluminum compositions or ferrous alloys is also an unproven extension in the supplied evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is the integration of extraordinary ambient-temperature deformation with economical, component-scale manufacturing. In the documented precursor, specialized preparation and high-pressure torsion produced a nanostructured alloy that was tested using miniature specimens. Bridging that result to large feedstock requires a way to create the necessary microstructure consistently throughout useful material volumes and retain it through storage, handling and forming. The paper’s aging-related property changes make microstructural stability a practical issue, rather than an assumption that can be taken for granted.

The deformation mechanism must also work at useful production rates. The reported maximum elongation occurred at a tensile strain rate of 5.5 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹, so it does not demonstrate rapid industrial forming. Grain-boundary engineering and the accommodation of grain-boundary sliding are relevant scientific questions, but evidence of that mechanism in the tested alloy is not evidence that it can deliver the same performance at higher rates, across large components or in other alloy families.

Engineering synthesis: a successful process would need to control deformation across real component geometries, avoid unacceptable local thinning or damage, and deliver consistent dimensions and properties. It would also need an economical preparation route for affordable compositions, followed by any necessary property restoration without losing the advantages of the forming process. Strength, fatigue resistance and durability must be qualified after the complete processing sequence; high elongation cannot substitute for those measurements.

current_state.text: Kaveh Edalati, Zenji Horita and Ruslan Z. Valiev’s 2018 paper, “Transition from poor ductility to room-temperature superplasticity in a nanostructured aluminum alloy,” Scientific Reports 8, 6740, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-018-25140-1, reported a maximum room-temperature tensile elongation of 480% in an Al–30 at.% Zn alloy processed using high-pressure torsion. This is a documented laboratory demonstration of room-temperature superplasticity in an aluminum alloy. The supplied review identifies the elongation result in Figure 1 and its accompanying results text; Figure 2 concerns surface evidence for grain-boundary sliding.

Processing used discs 10 mm in diameter and 0.8 mm thick, with high-pressure torsion at 6 GPa for 200 rotations at 1 rpm. Tensile specimens had gauge dimensions of 0.7 × 0.5 × 1.5 mm, and the maximum elongation was obtained at 5.5 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. Preparation also included homogenization. These details establish the small scale, intensive preparation and slow test conditions of the demonstration. They do not establish large-scale, high-throughput forming of ordinary commercial sheet, or equivalent behavior in ferrous alloys.

The paper discusses final-shape forming and subsequent heat treatment to increase flow stress. Those discussions support a possible manufacturing direction, while leaving the complete production route, finished-component qualification and economics undemonstrated by this source. The supplied evidence therefore establishes a laboratory precursor, while leaving the present-day availability of the broader manufacturing capability unresolved. The empty freshness record cannot establish whether later work has closed that gap.

The supplied review describes the retained eight-page main article as apparently complete, with its title, authors and DOI internally verified. Supplementary material and figure images were not supplied for inspection; the experimental assessment rests on the methods and results prose. The source index records untruncated text extraction without reported extraction issues, although the resolved retrieval URL contains a cookie-related error parameter. The exact publication day remains unconfirmed: the research gives 30 April 2018, but the retained article’s publication field is a placeholder. These access and metadata limitations do not invalidate the reported experiment.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent manufacturers should repeatedly form large, representative components from affordable aluminum or ferrous feedstock at ambient temperature and at rates useful for a specified commercial application. Reports should identify alloy composition, feedstock dimensions, preparation history, forming conditions, component geometry, dimensional accuracy, rejection rate and production yield. Demonstrating one alloy family would establish that scope; it would not automatically establish the other.
completion_criteria.label: Repeatable ambient-temperature forming of large components at commercially useful rates

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: results should be reproduced across batches, operators and manufacturing sites, with the workable ranges of composition, storage time, temperature, strain rate and component geometry stated explicitly. Cost and energy accounting should include feedstock preparation, forming, rejected material and subsequent treatments. Comparisons with the relevant existing production route should show where the process offers a practical advantage. Finite demonstrations would establish breadth within tested conditions, not universal formability across common alloys.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible manufacturing with explicit practical boundaries and comparative resource accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed product qualification: components should meet application-specific strength, fatigue and durability requirements after the complete forming and treatment sequence. Any restoration of structural properties should be demonstrated on the finished parts, including its effects on dimensions and consistency. This requirement addresses the paper’s explicit warning about low flow stress and its discussion of subsequent heat treatment; the proposed qualification program is not an established standard supplied by that paper.
completion_criteria.label: Finished components meet application-specific strength, fatigue and durability requirements

completion_criteria.text: An elongation greater than 1,000% may be retained as an optional illustrative ambition. It is not a universal completion threshold, and its historical provenance is not established by the supplied evidence. Component-level formability, speed, repeatability, economics and finished properties would be more convincing evidence of the proposed manufacturing capability than a single exceptional tensile-elongation value.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Demonstrated tensile elongation greater than 1,000%

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MET-01, “Predictive metallurgy from composition to lifetime,” could help design compositions, microstructures and processing schedules for this forming capability and predict finished properties. Its objective is predictive understanding across a material’s life; MET-08 concerns a particular manufacturing capability. MET-07, “Manufacturable, damage-tolerant bulk metallic glasses,” also connects material structure with manufacturability, but addresses a different structural class. The supplied MET-08 precursor is a nanostructured crystalline alloy with grain-boundary-mediated deformation, rather than a bulk metallic glass.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-02, “Steel from ore without fossil carbon at competitive global scale,” addresses primary metal production, and MET-05, “Titanium at mass-market structural-metal cost,” addresses the economics of another structural metal. Either could complement broader manufacturing improvements, but neither establishes room-temperature superplastic forming of common alloys. MET-03, “Repeated, high-grade recycling of mixed steel scrap,” and MET-10, “Repeated upcycling of mixed aluminum scrap into demanding alloys,” concern feedstock recovery and quality. Recycled material could become an input to MET-08, but tolerance to its composition variability would need separate demonstration.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-04, “Structural metals that repeatedly heal fatigue damage in service,” concerns damage recovery during service. MET-08 instead concerns deformation during manufacture; its finished parts would still need fatigue qualification. MET-11, “Structural alloys with broadly reliable intrinsic corrosion resistance,” concerns environmental durability. Exceptional forming behavior does not establish corrosion resistance, and corrosion-resistant chemistry does not establish superplastic formability.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-06, “A practical structural alloy system for sustained fusion-reactor conditions,” and MET-09, “Uncoated structural alloys for very high temperatures in oxidizing environments,” target demanding service environments. Room-temperature forming could potentially assist fabrication of suitable materials, but their service requirements are separate from forming temperature. MET-08 does not establish fusion compatibility, high-temperature structural performance or oxidation resistance.

brief.title: Shaping common metals without heating them
possible: Manufacturers could shape affordable aluminum or iron-based alloys into complex parts at room temperature. The metal would stretch far without tearing, allowing large components to take their final shape at speeds useful for production.
why: This would give manufacturers another route to complex metal parts, with less heating during shaping and fewer fabrication steps. Parts formed close to their final shape could replace some assemblies made by joining separate pieces.

sources.who: Kaveh Edalati, Zenji Horita and Ruslan Z. Valiev
sources.showed: They demonstrated superplasticity, or exceptionally large stretching, at room temperature in an aluminum–zinc alloy. Its tiny internal crystals slid past each other, a process called grain-boundary sliding.
sources.quote:
We 
report the first observation of room-temperature superplasticity (over 400% tensile elongations) in a 
nanostructured Al alloy by enhanced grain-boundary sliding.
sources.cited_for: An aluminum alloy can stretch exceptionally far at room temperature.
sources.not_established: Miniature stretching tests do not establish fast, economical forming of large components.

sources.showed: They studied aluminum–zinc alloys processed by high-pressure torsion, which squeezes and twists metal. Zinc content changed the internal structure and how readily the metal deformed.
sources.quote: It was shown that in every case, HPT resulted decomposition in the microstructure, but there is a significant difference between the microstructures of alloys with low and high Zn content.
sources.cited_for: Alloy composition affects the structure and stretching behavior produced by intensive processing.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish a repeatable manufacturing route for large parts made from common alloys.

sources.who: M. Demirtas, H. Yanar and G. Purcek
sources.showed: Storage reduced how far a zinc-based alloy could stretch. Corrosion at the edges of its internal crystals helped holes form during stretching and caused early failure.
sources.quote:
Corroded 
grain boundaries resulted in cavity nucleation during the tensile tests and some of these cavities attained large sizes and caused 
premature failure.
sources.cited_for: Storage can change stretching performance, making material stability a practical requirement.
sources.not_established: Results in zinc-based alloys do not establish stable aluminum or iron-based feedstock for component manufacturing.

sources.showed: They produced an aluminum alloy with ultrafine grains, meaning very small internal crystals. It stretched exceptionally far when heated and retained high hardness afterward.
sources.quote:
AsaresultofHPT,asaturatedUFGmicrostructurehav-
ing an average grain size of 200nm was produced, as
showninFigure 1(a).
sources.cited_for: A commercial aluminum alloy can combine stretching at reduced temperatures with retained hardness.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish room-temperature shaping or finished-part resistance to repeated loads and long-term damage.

shown: Kaveh Edalati and colleagues achieved 480% stretching at room temperature in a specially prepared aluminum–zinc alloy. They tested miniature samples slowly after intensive squeezing and twisting.

Nguyen Q. Chinh and colleagues demonstrated exceptional stretching in a commercial aluminum alloy at 170°C, with high hardness retained afterward. This brings the behavior closer to useful alloys, while still requiring heat.
missing: An economical way to prepare large amounts of metal with an internal structure that stays suitable during storage and shaping remains to be demonstrated.
Large, complex parts must be formed repeatedly at commercially useful speeds without excessive thinning, damage or rejected parts.
Finished parts must meet strength, resistance to repeated loads and durability requirements after all necessary treatments.
The complete process must show a cost and energy advantage over the production route it would replace.

milestones.label: Large parts form reliably at useful speeds without heating
milestones.explanation: Independent manufacturers would have to repeatedly form large parts from affordable aluminum or iron-based alloys at room temperature and commercially useful speeds. This would establish practical shaping for the tested alloy family.

milestones.label: Manufacturing repeats across sites with clear costs and limits
milestones.explanation: Results would have to repeat across batches, operators and sites, with workable conditions defined and full-process cost and energy compared with existing routes. This would establish where the process offers a practical advantage.

milestones.label: Finished parts meet their strength and service requirements
milestones.explanation: Finished parts would have to meet application requirements for strength, repeated loading and durability after all treatments, while keeping consistent dimensions. This would establish that easy shaping produces usable components.

milestones.label: An optional stretching result exceeds 1,000%
milestones.explanation: A stretching test would have to exceed 1,000% elongation as an optional ambition. This would demonstrate greater stretch, while practical forming would still depend on speed, repeatability, economics and finished properties.

uncertain: Can the behavior extend from specially prepared aluminum–zinc alloys to ordinary commercial aluminum compositions or iron-based alloys?
Can faster shaping preserve exceptional stretch without causing local thinning or damage?
Will preparation and any later heat treatment preserve the cost and energy advantages of shaping at room temperature?

page.title: Room-temperature superplastic forming of aluminium alloys
page.definition: Aluminium-alloy sheet is shaped at 300 ± 2 K by superplastic flow: very large deformation distributed without local necking, or concentrated thinning. Feedstock is compatible with conventional rolling-mill production, and finished components meet their application specifications.

goal.need: Argonne reports 10–30% elongation during forming for typical aluminium sheet and strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻³ s⁻¹ for conventional superplastic forming. The industry roadmap describes forming near 500 °C. The 2018 room-temperature experiment reached 480% elongation at 300 ± 2 K, but at 5.5 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ in a specimen with a 1.5 mm gauge length. The industrial goals concern sheet manufacture and forming speed as well as ductility.

figures.caption: Conventional aluminium-forming conditions described in Argonne's 2007 report.

statements.body: The Aluminum Association, with support from the U.S. Department of Energy
statements.quote: compatible with sheet production in the high-volume environment of a conventional rolling mill.
statements.context: The Superplastic Forming section requests an alloy/fabrication process with this manufacturing compatibility; it does not specify room-temperature forming.

statements.quote:
An important current objective is therefore
to process materials which are capable of achieving
superplastic ductilities at high strain rates
statements.context: The joint research paper includes Superform USA coauthor A. J. Barnes. Its forming experiments used elevated temperature.

statements.body: Kyushu University, Ufa State Aviation Technical University and Saint Petersburg State University research team
statements.quote: room-temperature superplasticity provides a unique opportunity to shape the nanostructured materials to their final shape easily at room temperature.
statements.context: The developers' statement concerns final shaping; their reported experiment measured tensile deformation.

completion.title: A room-temperature superplastically formed aluminium component meets its application specification.
completion.criterion: A commercially specified aluminium alloy is supplied by a route compatible with conventional rolling-mill production and superplastically formed at 300 ± 2 K into a specified application component. After all treatments, the component meets pre-existing dimensional and mechanical acceptance requirements, and the forming operation meets the application's specified cycle time. The alloy, component and application specification delimit the achievement; no universal cost, yield or component-size cutoff is supplied by the sources.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of the industry feedstock goal, the published room-temperature experiment and application-specific qualification.
completion.basis: The Aluminum Association/DOE roadmap, Argonne report, JIS H 7007 and H 7504, and ASTM E2712 were searched for a joint room-temperature manufacturing acceptance test; none was found. The narrow test combines the roadmap's rolling-mill compatibility goal with a finished application component. The 300 ± 2 K condition comes from the aluminium experiment. Application requirements supply the remaining acceptance limits.

milestones.title: An aluminium alloy exceeds 400% tensile elongation at 300 ± 2 K.
milestones.criterion: Total tensile elongation exceeds 400% at 300 ± 2 K. On 30 April 2018, Edalati et al. reported 480% at 5.5 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ in Al–30 at.% Zn, using a 0.7 × 0.5 × 1.5 mm gauge after high-pressure torsion at 6 GPa for 200 rotations. Tensile replicate counts were not stated in the main article. A commercial Al–Zn–Mg–Zr alloy exceeded 500% at 170 °C and 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ in the paper published on 15 September 2021; that result required heating.
milestones.set_by: Superplasticity convention explicitly used by Edalati et al. in Scientific Reports; 300 ± 2 K is their experimental room-temperature condition, rather than a universal temperature definition.

milestones.title: An aluminium alloy exhibits superplasticity at a strain rate of at least 10⁻² s⁻¹.
milestones.criterion: Superplastic deformation occurs at a strain rate ≥10⁻² s⁻¹, meeting the JIS definition of high-strain-rate superplasticity. This rate milestone does not require room temperature. Horita et al. reported approximately 2280% elongation at 673 K and an initial strain rate of 3.3 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ in Al–3 wt.% Mg–0.2 wt.% Sc. Tensile specimens had a 5 mm gauge length and a 2 × 3 mm cross-section; replicate counts per condition were not specified.
milestones.set_by: Japanese Industrial Standards Committee, JIS H 7007:2002, section 4, general definitions table, entry for high-strain-rate superplasticity. The threshold is stated in a table.

milestones.title: Aluminium-alloy sheet forms an intact hemisphere with height approximately equal to radius at 300 ± 2 K.
milestones.criterion: Aluminium-alloy sheet no thicker than 3 mm reaches an intact hemispherical bulge, H/R ≈ 1, at 300 ± 2 K. H is bulge height and R is die-opening radius. JIS H 7504 supplies the geometry and sheet-thickness scope; it supplies no universal forming-time or thinning limit. No qualifying room-temperature result was located. Horita et al. illustrated two domes formed at 673 K for 30 and 60 s from approximately 0.3 mm discs with a 7 mm exposed diameter; those heated demonstrations do not establish this milestone.
milestones.set_by: Atlas application of the JIS H 7504:2003 hemispherical endpoint to room temperature. Searches of JIS H 7504 and ASTM E2712 found no published room-temperature prototype acceptance criterion; this temperature-specific milestone is an Atlas synthesis.

not_found: No outside body was found to define a joint acceptance test covering room-temperature forming, rolling-mill-compatible feedstock, production rate and finished-component properties.
No published room-temperature aluminium-sheet hemisphere demonstration or application-qualified production component was located.
No published room-temperature forming target for common ferrous alloys, or quantitative definition of common alloy chemistry, was located.
Tensile replicate counts were not established from the main articles reporting the cited 2000, 2018 and 2021 results.
ASTM E2448-22 could not be opened; the accessible ASTM E2712-22 page provided its scope and significance rather than the complete standard.
